title: Observe a User Problem
why: Observed context keeps a design problem grounded in an actual user need.
activity: Choose an everyday task. Observe its context with consent and list evidence, assumptions, constraints, and a desired outcome.
evidence: An anonymized context map and problem brief.
reflection: Which observation supports your problem statement?

title: Plan and Conduct Research
why: A clear research question makes it easier to choose a useful method.
activity: Define a research question and method. Speak with at least three consenting people, avoid identifying notes, and distinguish observations from interpretations.
evidence: A research plan, discussion guide, and anonymized observations.
reflection: Which finding challenged your original assumption?

title: Organize the Experience
why: Content organization determines whether users can find what they need.
activity: Inventory the content needed for the task. Propose grouping and navigation, then ask someone to find key information.
evidence: A content hierarchy, navigation map, and findability findings.
reflection: Which label or grouping confused the person evaluating it?

title: Design the Full Interaction
why: A usable interaction includes errors, feedback, and recovery as well as success.
activity: Map the happy path, empty state, error, cancellation, and recovery. Explain the feedback users receive at each transition.
evidence: A task flow and state-by-state wireframes.
reflection: Which failure state required a different interaction?

title: Establish Visual Foundations
why: Shared visual rules improve consistency and help prevent inaccessible states.
activity: Define typography, spacing, color roles, and reusable controls. Check contrast and demonstrate focus, selected, disabled, and error states.
evidence: A small token system and accessible component/state sheet.
reflection: Which component state was hardest to make clear without color alone?

title: Prototype a Testable Task
why: A prototype should answer a question before it becomes a polished presentation.
activity: Connect the main flow in an interactive prototype. Choose fidelity based on your research question and make key failures testable.
evidence: A runnable prototype and clearly stated assumptions to test.
reflection: What can this prototype test, and what can it not test?

title: Evaluate Usability
why: Task observations reveal where a design prevents people from reaching their goal.
activity: Run task-based sessions with at least three consenting people. Record completion observations and issue severity without inventing metrics or generalizing the sample.
evidence: Anonymized task findings and a prioritized issue list.
reflection: Which issue had the strongest evidence of user impact?

title: Iterate From Evidence
why: Iteration connects design changes to observed problems rather than personal preference.
activity: Address the highest-impact observed issues and compare before/after interactions. Recheck contrast, labels, and recovery behavior.
evidence: An iteration comparison linked to research evidence.
reflection: What evidence supports the change you made?

title: Prepare a Useful Handoff
why: Handoff succeeds when collaborators can implement behavior without guessing.
activity: Specify components, layout behavior, states, content, accessibility, and open questions. Ask a developer or peer to identify unclear decisions.
evidence: A handoff specification with feedback and resolved questions.
reflection: Which question from the reviewer exposed a missing specification?

title: Tell the Design Story
why: A design case study should make the reasoning visible alongside the final screens.
activity: Create a case study connecting the problem, research, interaction choices, visual system, test findings, and limitations. Separate your contribution from team work.
evidence: A design case study with prototype, evidence, iterations, and reflection.
reflection: Which decision would you revisit with more research?
